## Objectives {.unnumbered}

- Have a good grasp of `R` code, including:
    - Basic syntax
    - Basic numeric data types (floats, vectors, matrices)
    - Data frames
    - Control flow
    - Functions, including higher-order functions
    - Understanding error messages and debugging
- Be able to write and interpret the output of `R` code covering each of the above.

::: {.callout-note}
## Solutions

This is the solutions version of the worksheet. Each task is followed by one worked solution; in most cases other correct answers are possible. We use the idiomatic `<-` for assignment throughout, though `=` also works.
:::

## Part 1: R Fundamentals

### Tasks

- [x] Print "Hello World" to the console.
- [x] Write a function that takes a name, and prints "Hello <name>" to the console.
- [x] Assign the value 42 to a variable called `answer`.
- [x] Create a numeric vector containing the numbers 1 through 5.
- [x] Create a numeric vector containing the numbers 1 through 1000.
- [x] Create a matrix with 10 rows and 10 columns filled with numbers 1 to 100.
- [x] Create a data frame with two columns: one called `name` containing three names, and one called `age` containing three ages.
- [x] Write a function that returns the square of its input.
- [x] Use a for loop to print the numbers 1 to 5.
- [x] Use a for loop to compute the mean of a numeric vector.

```{r}
# Print "Hello World"
print("Hello World")

# A function that greets a name
greet <- function(name) {
    cat("Hello", name, "\n")
}
greet("Ada")

# Assign 42 to answer. The idiomatic operator is <-, but `answer = 42` works too.
answer <- 42

# Numeric vectors
one_to_five <- 1:5
one_to_thousand <- 1:1000

# A 10x10 matrix filled with 1 to 100
m <- matrix(1:100, nrow = 10, ncol = 10)

# A data frame with names and ages
df <- data.frame(
    name = c("Ada", "Alan", "Grace"),
    age = c(36, 41, 27)
)

# A function returning the square of its input
square <- function(x) {
    x^2
}
square(7)

# A for loop printing 1 to 5
for (i in 1:5) {
    print(i)
}

# A for loop computing the mean of a numeric vector
nums <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)
total <- 0
for (n in nums) {
    total <- total + n
}
total / length(nums)
```

## Part 1b: Lists

Recall that a *list* can hold a mixture of types, and that lists turn up all over `R` — in particular, they are how a function returns several results at once, and how we store a collection of records.

- [x] A function can only return a single object, so when we want to return several results we bundle them into a list. Write a function `summarise_vector(x)` that returns a **named list** with the `mean`, `min`, `max`, and `n` (length) of a numeric vector `x`. Call it on `c(210, 217, 230, 205)` and use `$` to print just the mean from the result.
- [x] Call `str()` on the value your function returns to confirm its structure, then modify `summarise_vector` so that missing values are ignored (test it on a vector containing `NA`).

```{r}
# The `na.rm = TRUE` arguments handle the second part of the task: with them,
# missing values are ignored by mean/min/max.
summarise_vector <- function(x) {
    list(
        mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
        min = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
        max = max(x, na.rm = TRUE),
        n = length(x)
    )
}

result <- summarise_vector(c(210, 217, 230, 205))
result$mean

# str() confirms the structure: a named list of four numbers
str(result)

# The na.rm = TRUE means NA values are ignored
summarise_vector(c(210, 217, NA, 205))$mean
```

- [x] Below is a list of penguins, each itself a list. Using a `for` loop (or `sapply`), extract the `species` of every penguin into a character vector, and compute the mean flipper length across all of them.

```{r}
penguins <- list(
    list(name = "Flipper", species = "Adelie",  flipper = 210),
    list(name = "Tux",     species = "Gentoo",  flipper = 217),
    list(name = "Pingu",   species = "Emperor", flipper = 230)
)
```

```{r}
# sapply is the concise way; it applies the function to each penguin and
# simplifies the results to a vector.
species <- sapply(penguins, function(p) p$species)
species

mean(sapply(penguins, function(p) p$flipper))
```

- [x] The function below is supposed to extract the name of every penguin. Examine its output on the two lists, `penguins` and `penguins2`. Why does it not return the expected values for `penguins2`? Fix the code so it correctly returns penguin names.

```{r}
penguins2 <- list(
    list(name = "Flipper", species = "Adelie",  flipper = 210),
    list(species = "Gentoo", flipper = 217, name = "Tux"),
    list(flipper = 230, name = "Pingu", species = "Emperor")
)
```

The original used `penguin[[1]]`, which accesses the element by **position**. That
only works when `name` is the first element of every record, which is not the case
in `penguins2`. Accessing by **name** with `penguin$name` (or `penguin[["name"]]`)
is robust to the order in which the fields are stored.

```{r}
get_penguin_names <- function(penguins) {
    sapply(penguins, function(penguin) penguin$name)
}

get_penguin_names(penguins)
get_penguin_names(penguins2)
```

## Part 2: Advanced Array Indexing

In the lecture we saw that we can use *logical indexing* into arrays, i.e.

```{r}
vector <- c(1,2,3,4,5)
elements <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
vector[elements]
```


We can also do *elementwise comparisons*:

```{r}
vector > 3
vector[vector > 3]
```

Consider next this vector:

```{r}
vector <- 1:100
```

Use elementwise indexing to display all elements in the vector that are:

- [x] $\leq$ 10
- [x] $>$ 90
- [x] $\leq 10$ or $> 90$
- [x] $> 10$ and $\leq 90$
- [x] Odd
- [x] (Advanced): Prime

Conditions are combined with `&` (and) and `|` (or) — note these are the
*vectorised* versions, which act elementwise, unlike `&&` and `||`.

```{r}
vector[vector <= 10]
vector[vector > 90]
vector[vector <= 10 | vector > 90]
vector[vector > 10 & vector <= 90]

# Odd numbers: those with remainder 1 when divided by 2
vector[vector %% 2 == 1]
```

For the primes, we write a helper that tests a single number, then use `sapply`
to build a logical vector we can index with. A number is prime if it is at least
2 and has no divisors other than 1 and itself.

```{r}
is_prime <- function(n) {
    if (n < 2) return(FALSE)
    if (n == 2) return(TRUE)
    # TRUE if none of 2..(n-1) divide n exactly
    !any(n %% 2:(n - 1) == 0)
}

vector[sapply(vector, is_prime)]
```

## Part 3: Control Flow

### Part (a): Conditionals

In data science we very often want to make the *same* decision for every element of a vector or column. Writing a for loop with an `if` inside would work, but the *vectorised* conditionals `if_else` and `case_when` are cleaner and faster. Both come from `dplyr`, so load it first:

```{r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)
```

We will apply them to the following data frame of students and their exam scores:

```{r}
students <- data.frame(
    name = c("Ada", "Alan", "Grace", "Edsger", "Katherine"),
    score = c(72, 65, 43, 38, 91)
)
```

- [x] Using `if_else`, add a new column `result` to `students` that is `"pass"` when the score is at least 40 and `"fail"` otherwise.
- [x] Using `case_when`, add a new column `grade` to `students` giving the classification: `"first"` (at least 70), `"2:1"` (at least 60), `"2:2"` (at least 50), `"third"` (at least 40), and `"fail"` otherwise. Remember that conditions are checked in order, so the most specific should come first.

```{r}
students$result <- if_else(students$score >= 40, "pass", "fail")

# Conditions are checked top to bottom, so the highest thresholds come first.
# TRUE acts as the catch-all "else" branch.
students$grade <- case_when(
    students$score >= 70 ~ "first",
    students$score >= 60 ~ "2:1",
    students$score >= 50 ~ "2:2",
    students$score >= 40 ~ "third",
    TRUE ~ "fail"
)

students
```

- [x] Standard `if`/`else` statements make a single decision about a single value. Using `if`, `else if` and `else`, complete the stub function `is_leap_year` below so that it returns `TRUE` if `year` is a *leap year* and `FALSE` otherwise. The rule is:
    - if `year` is divisible by 400, it is a leap year;
    - otherwise, if `year` is divisible by 100, it is *not* a leap year;
    - otherwise, if `year` is divisible by 4, it is a leap year;
    - otherwise, it is *not* a leap year.

::: {.callout-tip}
The modulo operator `%%` gives the remainder of a division, so `year %% 400 == 0` tests whether `year` is divisible by 400.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## `stopifnot`

`stopifnot()` is a handy way to check your work. Given one or more conditions, it does nothing if they are all `TRUE`, but raises an error as soon as one is `FALSE`. So once your function is correct the chunk below will run silently; until then, the first failing check tells you which case is wrong.
:::

```{r}
# The order of the branches matches the rule: 400 first, then 100, then 4.
is_leap_year <- function(year) {
    if (year %% 400 == 0) {
        TRUE
    } else if (year %% 100 == 0) {
        FALSE
    } else if (year %% 4 == 0) {
        TRUE
    } else {
        FALSE
    }
}

# Self-check: runs without error now that is_leap_year is correct
stopifnot(
    is_leap_year(2000) == TRUE,   # divisible by 400
    is_leap_year(2024) == TRUE,   # divisible by 4, not by 100
    is_leap_year(1900) == FALSE,  # divisible by 100, not by 400
    is_leap_year(2100) == FALSE   # divisible by 100, not by 400
)
```

### Part (b): Loops

- [x] In the next block, write a function that uses a for loop to print a message if an input vector contains NA values. Test it on the five variables supplied below.

```{r}
vec1 <- 1:10
vec2 <- c(1,2,NA,4)
vec3 <- c()
vec4 <- "This is not a vector"
vec5 <- matrix(c(1,2,3,4,NA,6), nrow=2, ncol=3)
```

```{r}
# Looping over the elements and checking each with is.na(). We return as soon as
# we find one, so the message is printed at most once.
check_for_na <- function(v) {
    for (element in v) {
        if (is.na(element)) {
            cat("The vector contains NA values.\n")
            return(invisible())
        }
    }
    cat("No NA values found.\n")
}

check_for_na(vec1)
check_for_na(vec2)
check_for_na(vec3)  # empty: the loop body never runs, so "No NA values found."
check_for_na(vec4)
check_for_na(vec5)  # a matrix is a vector under the hood, so this works too
```

- [x] In a new chunk, write a function called `make_square` that, given an integer, will print a square of full stops with side length that integer.

```{r}
# The first and last rows are solid; the rows in between have a dot at each end
# and spaces in the middle. strrep() repeats a string a given number of times.
make_square <- function(n) {
    for (i in 1:n) {
        if (i == 1 || i == n) {
            cat(strrep(".", n), "\n", sep = "")
        } else {
            cat(".", strrep(" ", n - 2), ".", "\n", sep = "")
        }
    }
}

make_square(3)
make_square(5)
```

- [x] (Advanced): Look up *while loops* in `R`. Write a function that uses a while loop to simulate a particle undergoing a *random walk* in 1D. Terminate the walk when the particle reaches either -10 or +10, and print where it ended up and how many steps it took.
- [x] (Advanced): Run your function from above multiple times. Display how often the particle ended at -10 and how often it ended at +10. Make sure that your results do not change if the worksheet is run multiple times!

::: {.callout-tip}
Your random walk uses randomly generated numbers, so it will produce different output every time the document is rendered. To make results *reproducible* — the same every time — look up `set.seed()` and call it once at the start of the chunk. We will return to why this matters for reproducibility later in the course.
:::

```{r}
# sample(c(-1, 1), 1) picks one of -1 or +1 with equal probability.
# The while loop continues as long as the particle is strictly inside (-10, 10).
random_walk <- function() {
    x <- 0
    steps <- 0
    while (x > -10 && x < 10) {
        x <- x + sample(c(-1, 1), 1)
        steps <- steps + 1
    }
    list(end = x, steps = steps)
}

# set.seed makes the "random" numbers reproducible: the same every render.
set.seed(42)

walk <- random_walk()
cat("The particle ended at", walk$end, "after", walk$steps, "steps.\n")

# Run it many times and tabulate where it ended up. By symmetry the two
# outcomes should be roughly equally likely.
ends <- sapply(1:1000, function(i) random_walk()$end)
table(ends)
```

## Part 4: Pipes

The *pipe* operator `|>` passes the value on its left into the first argument of the function on its right. Chaining pipes lets a sequence of nested function calls be read left-to-right, in the order they actually happen, rather than inside-out.

- [x] Rewrite the nested expression below using `|>`, so that it reads as a left-to-right pipeline. Check that your piped version gives the same answer. (Note that the last call takes an extra argument — recall that the piped value fills only the *first* argument of each function.)

```{r}
x <- c(4, 9, 16, 25)
round(mean(sqrt(x)), 1)
```

Reading the nested call from the inside out, we take `sqrt`, then `mean`, then
`round`. The pipe lets us write that in the same order. The `1` becomes the
*second* argument of `round`, since the piped value fills the first.

```{r}
x |> sqrt() |> mean() |> round(1)
```

## Part 5: Debugging

In this section we will look at some pathologies of `R` that might require some more work to figure out.
First, try to solve the problems using Google or `R` help files.
Then, feed the problem into an LLM and see whether it comes up with the same solution, a better one (or a worse one!)

### Tasks

- [x] Modify the below code to return the row sums of only the non-NA values.

```{r}
# A data frame with some missing values
df <- data.frame(a = c(1, 2, 3, NA, 5), b = c(10, NA, 30, 40, 50))
```

`apply(df, 1, sum)` returns `NA` for any row containing an `NA`, because
`sum()` propagates missing values by default. Passing `na.rm = TRUE` (which
`apply` forwards to `sum`) ignores them instead.

```{r}
row_sums <- apply(df, 1, sum, na.rm = TRUE)
print(row_sums)
```

- [x] Given two vectors `x` and `y` of the same length, the below code prints out the (Euclidean) distance between `x` and `y`, but for some reason it is printing a distance between vectors that are not of the same length. Correct the code.

The problem is *recycling*: when `x` and `y` have different lengths, `R`
silently repeats the shorter one to match the longer (here `b` becomes
`c(5, 6, 5, 6)`), so `x - y` computes something meaningless without complaint.
The fix is a guard clause that stops with a clear error when the lengths differ,
rather than returning a wrong answer.

```{r}
#| error: true
distance <- function(x, y) {
    if (length(x) != length(y)) {
        stop("x and y must be the same length")
    }
    norm(x - y, type = "2")
}

a <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
b <- c(5, 6)

# This now raises a clear error instead of silently recycling:
distance(a, b)
```

```{r}
# On vectors of equal length it works as intended:
distance(c(1, 2, 3, 4), c(5, 6, 7, 8))
```

- [x] The below code prints out "values are equal" if `a` and `b` are equal, but for some reason it is not working for these example values. Correct the code.

Because doubles are stored to finite precision, `0.1 + 0.2` is not *exactly*
`0.3`, so `==` returns `FALSE`. Comparing with `all.equal()`, which allows a
tiny tolerance, gives the intended result. We wrap it in `isTRUE()` because
`all.equal()` returns a *message* rather than `FALSE` when the values differ,
which would not behave correctly inside `if`.

```{r}
a <- 0.1 + 0.2
b <- 0.3

if (isTRUE(all.equal(a, b))) {
    print("Values are equal.")
} else {
    print("Values are not equal.")
}
```

Hint: see the [Assignments and Types](https://soton-fds.github.io/week02.html#assignments-and-types) section of the notes.

- [x] The below returns the entries of `vec1` for which `vec2 == "y"`. So why does `subset` contain an `NA`? Fix the code.

```{r}
vec1 <- 1:5
vec2 <- c("x", "y", NA, "x", "y")
```

The comparison `vec2 == "y"` is `NA` wherever `vec2` is `NA` (an unknown value
is not known to equal `"y"`), and indexing a vector with `NA` yields an `NA`
element. Using `which()` returns only the positions that are `TRUE`, discarding
the `NA`; equivalently we could write `vec2 == "y" & !is.na(vec2)`.

```{r}
subset <- vec1[which(vec2 == "y")]
subset
```
